# Packages and data

This file builds on `mutationAnalysis.Rmd`, which cleans the clinical data,
defines the cohort of 1,006 patients with clinical, mutation and expression
data, filters to non-synonymous mutations and saves the objects to
`processed/report1_objects.rds`. We load the same file used by
`investigation2.Rmd` so the analyses use the same patients and mutation calls.

```{r inv3-packages}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11))

# Keep the same colours for the three panels in every figure.
pathway_cols <- c("PI3K/AKT" = "#1F5D88",
                  "p53/DNA damage response" = "#B14A39",
                  "MAPK/JNK" = "#6A558D")
```

```{r inv3-load}
report1 <- readRDS("processed/report1_objects.rds")
cohort <- report1$cohort
mut_ns <- report1$mut_ns

dim(cohort)
table(cohort$SUBTYPE, useNA = "ifany")
```

Question: does the frequency of mutations in selected pathway gene panels
differ between PAM50 breast cancer subtypes, and how much of each panel's
result comes from its most frequently mutated gene?

# Define the pathway gene panels

Mutations in different genes can affect the same biological process.
We therefore group selected genes into three panels based on the breast
cancer signalling pathways discussed by TCGA [1]. These panels represent
selected parts of PI3K/AKT signalling, the p53/DNA damage response and
MAPK/JNK signalling.

```{r inv3-panels}
pathway_genes <- list(
  "PI3K/AKT" = c("PIK3CA", "PIK3R1", "PTEN", "AKT1"),
  "p53/DNA damage response" = c("TP53", "ATM", "CHEK2"),
  "MAPK/JNK" = c("MAP3K1", "MAP2K4")
)

panel_genes <- data.frame(
  Panel = names(pathway_genes),
  Genes = vapply(pathway_genes, paste, collapse = ", ", FUN.VALUE = character(1))
)
knitr::kable(panel_genes, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Selected genes used to define each panel")
```

A patient has a panel mutation if their tumour has at least one
non-synonymous call in any of the selected genes. For example, a patient
with both TP53 and ATM mutations counts once in the p53/DNA damage response
panel. The same patient can count in more than one panel. This approach
also prevents repeated mutation records from counting the same patient
more than once within a panel.

# Keep patients with a known PAM50 subtype

PAM50 classifies tumours using gene expression. We use the recorded subtype
labels to compare mutation frequencies. Patients without a subtype label
are excluded from this investigation.

```{r inv3-subtypes}
subtype_levels <- c("LumA", "LumB", "Her2", "Basal", "Normal")
subtype_names <- c("Luminal A", "Luminal B", "HER2-enriched",
                    "Basal-like", "Normal-like")

subtype_df <- cohort %>%
  mutate(SUBTYPE = factor(sub("^BRCA_", "", as.character(SUBTYPE)),
                          levels = subtype_levels)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(SUBTYPE))

c(kept = nrow(subtype_df), removed = nrow(cohort) - nrow(subtype_df))
subtype_summary <- subtype_df %>% count(SUBTYPE, name = "Patients")
knitr::kable(subtype_summary, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Patients with a recorded PAM50 subtype")
```

Based on the output above, we keep `r nrow(subtype_df)` patients and exclude
`r nrow(cohort) - nrow(subtype_df)` without a recognised subtype. The groups
contain 499 Luminal A, 197 Luminal B, 78 HER2-enriched, 171 Basal-like and
36 Normal-like tumours. The group sizes differ substantially, so we compare
the percentage mutated within each subtype.

# Assign mutation status to each panel

We create one record per patient and panel. Status is either
"Panel mutation" or "No panel mutation" and is based on the
non-synonymous calls retained during the shared data preparation.

```{r inv3-status}
pathway_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(pathway_genes), function(panel) {
  # Membership checks count patients once, regardless of repeated calls.
  mutated_patients <- mut_ns$PATIENT_ID[
    mut_ns$Hugo_Symbol %in% pathway_genes[[panel]]]

  subtype_df %>%
    select(PATIENT_ID, SUBTYPE) %>%
    mutate(Pathway = panel,
           STATUS = ifelse(PATIENT_ID %in% mutated_patients,
                           "Panel mutation", "No panel mutation"))
})) %>%
  mutate(Pathway = factor(Pathway, levels = names(pathway_genes)),
         STATUS = factor(STATUS,
                         levels = c("No panel mutation", "Panel mutation")))

panel_summary <- pathway_df %>%
  group_by(Pathway) %>%
  summarise(Patients = n(),
            Mutated = sum(STATUS == "Panel mutation"),
            Percent = round(100 * Mutated / Patients, 1),
            .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(panel_summary, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Panel mutations among patients with a known subtype")
```

Based on the output above, 423 of 981 patients have a mutation in the
PI3K/AKT panel, 366 in the p53/DNA damage response panel and 127 in the
MAPK/JNK panel. These totals can overlap because patients may have
mutations in several panels.

# Mutation frequencies by PAM50 subtype

For each panel, we divide the number of patients with a mutation by the
total number of patients in that subtype. The bars use these percentages,
and the subtype sample sizes are shown below the x-axis.

```{r inv3-frequencies, fig.height=4.6}
pathway_freq <- pathway_df %>%
  group_by(Pathway, SUBTYPE) %>%
  summarise(Patients = n(),
            Mutated = sum(STATUS == "Panel mutation"),
            Percent = 100 * Mutated / Patients,
            .groups = "drop")

subtype_ticks <- setNames(
  paste0(subtype_names, "\n(n = ", subtype_summary$Patients, ")"),
  subtype_levels)

ggplot(pathway_freq, aes(x = SUBTYPE, y = Percent, fill = Pathway)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.72) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pathway_cols) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = subtype_ticks) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), breaks = seq(0, 100, 20),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.03))) +
  labs(title = "Pathway panel mutation frequencies by PAM50 subtype",
       x = "PAM50 subtype", y = "Patients with a panel mutation (%)",
       fill = "Panel") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9))
```

```{r inv3-frequency-table}
frequency_table <- pathway_freq %>%
  mutate(Result = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", Mutated, Percent)) %>%
  select(SUBTYPE, Pathway, Result) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Pathway, values_from = Result) %>%
  left_join(subtype_summary, by = "SUBTYPE") %>%
  select(SUBTYPE, Patients, all_of(names(pathway_genes)))

knitr::kable(frequency_table, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Subtype", "Patients", "PI3K/AKT",
                           "p53/DNA damage", "MAPK/JNK"),
             caption = "Patients with a panel mutation, n (% within subtype)")
```

From the plot, we can see that the panels have different subtype patterns.
The p53/DNA damage response panel is mutated in 89.5% of Basal-like and
73.1% of HER2-enriched tumours, compared with 12.8% of Luminal A tumours.
PI3K/AKT mutations are most common in Luminal A tumours (56.9%) and least
common in Basal-like tumours (14.0%). MAPK/JNK mutations also occur most
often in Luminal A tumours (19.8%). These patterns are consistent with the
subtype differences discussed in the TCGA breast cancer study [1].

# Test associations with PAM50 subtype

We test mutation status against subtype separately for each panel. A
simulated chi-square test avoids relying on the large-sample approximation
when a subtype has a small expected count. We then apply
Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction across the three panel tests.

```{r inv3-tests}
set.seed(310)
pathway_tests <- bind_rows(lapply(names(pathway_genes), function(panel) {
  panel_df <- filter(pathway_df, Pathway == panel)
  tab <- table(panel_df$SUBTYPE, panel_df$STATUS)
  test <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 99999)

  data.frame(Panel = panel,
             Chi_square = unname(test$statistic),
             p = test$p.value)
})) %>%
  mutate(p_adj_BH = p.adjust(p, method = "BH"))

knitr::kable(pathway_tests, digits = 5, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Panel mutation status vs subtype (BH-adjusted)")
```

Based on the output above, mutation status is associated with PAM50 subtype
for all three panels after BH correction (adjusted p < 0.001 for each).
The test compares all five subtypes together. Identifying which individual
subtype pairs differ would require additional comparisons.

With 99,999 simulations, the smallest possible raw p-value is 0.00001.
This is the simulation resolution. It limits how precisely we can describe
very strong associations, and BH correction may increase this value.

# Which genes contribute most to the panel results?

A panel's pattern may mainly reflect one frequently mutated gene. We
compare each panel's total with the number of patients carrying a mutation
in its most frequently mutated gene: PIK3CA, TP53 or MAP3K1.

```{r inv3-gene-contribution}
dominant_genes <- c("PI3K/AKT" = "PIK3CA",
                    "p53/DNA damage response" = "TP53",
                    "MAPK/JNK" = "MAP3K1")

gene_contribution <- bind_rows(lapply(names(dominant_genes), function(panel) {
  gene <- dominant_genes[[panel]]
  gene_patients <- mut_ns$PATIENT_ID[mut_ns$Hugo_Symbol == gene]
  n_gene <- sum(subtype_df$PATIENT_ID %in% gene_patients)
  n_panel <- panel_summary$Mutated[panel_summary$Pathway == panel]

  data.frame(Panel = panel, Gene = gene,
             Gene_mutated = n_gene, Panel_mutated = n_panel,
             Pct_of_panel = round(100 * n_gene / n_panel, 1))
}))
knitr::kable(gene_contribution, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Contribution of the most frequently mutated panel gene")
```

Based on the output above, TP53 is mutated in 342 of the 366 patients with
a p53/DNA damage response panel mutation (93.4%). PIK3CA accounts for
341 of 423 PI3K/AKT-positive patients (80.6%), and MAP3K1 for 87 of
127 MAPK/JNK-positive patients (68.5%). The p53 panel result is therefore
dominated by TP53. Other genes add patients to each panel, but grouping
genes does not make the result independent of the most common driver.

# Summary and limitations

- Mutation frequencies in all three selected panels differ across PAM50
  subtypes after BH correction (adjusted p < 0.001 for each).
- Basal-like and HER2-enriched tumours have the highest p53/DNA damage
  response panel mutation frequencies. Luminal A tumours have the highest
  PI3K/AKT and MAPK/JNK panel mutation frequencies.
- The p53 panel pattern is mainly driven by TP53, which accounts for
  93.4% of patients with a mutation in that panel.
- The panels contain selected genes and differ in size. They do not
  measure every possible alteration in a pathway, and larger gene sets
  have more opportunities to contain a mutation.
- Mutation status alone cannot establish whether a pathway is activated
  or suppressed. This analysis does not measure copy number changes,
  protein abundance or phosphorylation. Expression analysis in Report 2
  can provide additional evidence about biological effects.
- Twenty-five patients lack a subtype label, and the Normal-like group
  contains only 36 patients. These limitations affect the scope and
  precision of the subtype comparisons.

# Reference

[1] The Cancer Genome Atlas Network, "Comprehensive molecular portraits of
human breast tumours," Nature, vol. 490, no. 7418, pp. 61-70, 2012.
doi:10.1038/nature11412.
